title: God known by the mind made in his image
source_text: Νοῦν τοίνυν ἢ ἐπέκεινα νοῦ καὶ οὐσίας λέγοντες εἶναι ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀσώματον τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν. οὐκ ἂν ἄλλῳ τινὶ ἢ τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἐκείνου τοῦ νοῦ εἰκόνα γενομένῳ φήσομεν καταλαμβάνεσθαι τὸν θεόν· νῦν μὲν, ἵνα τῇ λέξει χρήσωμαι τοῦ Παύλου, „δι᾿ ἐσόπτρου καὶ (ἐν) αἰνίγματι τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον.“ „πρόσωπον“ δὲ ἐὰν λέγω. μὴ συκοφαντείτω τις διὰ τὴν λέξιν τὸν δηλούμενον νοῦν ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς, ἀλλὰ μανθανέτω (ἐν τῷ) „ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπῳ τὴν δόξαν κυρίου κατοπτριζόμενοι καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν εἰκόνα μεταμορφούμενοι ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν“ οὐ πρόσωπον αἰσθητὸν ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις παραλαμβανόμενον ἀλλὰ κατὰ τροπολογίαν νοούμενον ὡς καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ ὦτα. καὶ ὅσα ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ὁμώνυμα τοῖς τοῦ σώματος μέλεσι παρεστήσαμεν. καὶ ἄνθρωπος μὲν οὖν, τουτέστι ψυχὴ χρωμένη σώματι, λεγομένη „ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος“ ἀλλὰ καὶ „ψυχὴ,“ ἀποκρίνεται οὐχ ἅπερ Κέλσος ἀνέγραψεν, ἀλλ᾿ ἅπερ αὐτὸς διδάσκει ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος. σαρκὸς δὲ φωνῇ οὐκ ἂν Χριστιανὸς χρήσαιτο, μαθὼν „πνεύματι τὰς πράξεις τοῦ σώματος“ θανατοῦν καὶ „πάντοτε τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι“ περιφέρειν καὶ „νεκρώσατε τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς,“ καὶ εἰδὼς τί δηλοῦται ἐκ τοῦ „οὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τούτοις εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς σάρκας,“ ἐπιστάμενος δὲ καὶ ὅτι „οἱ ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντες θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται“ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πάντα πράττων εἰς τὸ μηδαμῶς αὐτὸν ἔτι εἶναι „ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἀλλ᾿“ „ἐν“ μόνῳ „τῷ πνεύματι.“
pass_a_gloss: Saying then that the God of the wholes (ὁ τῶν ὅλων θεός) is mind (νοῦς) or beyond (ἐπέκεινα) mind and being (οὐσία), simple (ἁπλοῦς), invisible (ἀόρατος), incorporeal (ἀσώματος), we would say God is apprehended (καταλαμβάνω) by nothing other than what has come to be according to the image (εἰκών) of that mind; now, to use the word (λέξις) of Paul, through a mirror (ἔσοπτρον) and in a riddle (αἴνιγμα), then face (πρόσωπον) to face. If I say 'face', let none slander (συκοφαντέω) on account of the word the sense (νοῦς) shown by it, but let him learn (from) 'with unveiled (ἀνακαλύπτω) face beholding as in a mirror (κατοπτρίζομαι) the glory (δόξα) of the Lord and transformed (μεταμορφόω) into the same image from glory to glory' that not a sensible (αἰσθητός) face is taken in such, but understood by tropology/figure (τροπολογία), as eyes and ears and whatever above we presented as homonymous (ὁμώνυμος) with the members (μέλος) of the body. And man, i.e. soul using a body, called 'the inner man' (ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος) and also 'soul', answers not what Celsus wrote (ἀναγράφω) but what the man of God himself teaches. A Christian would not use a voice of flesh, having learned by the Spirit (πνεῦμα) to put to death (θανατόω) the deeds (πρᾶξις) of the body and always to carry about (περιφέρω) the deadness/dying (νέκρωσις) of Jesus in the body, and 'put to death (νεκρόω) the members upon the earth', and knowing what is shown by 'my Spirit shall not remain (καταμένω) in these men for ever because they are flesh (σάρκες)', understanding also that those in flesh cannot please (ἀρέσκω) God, and therefore doing all so as no longer at all to be in the flesh but in the Spirit only.
pass_b_english: We say, then, that the God of the universe is mind, or beyond mind and being, simple, invisible and without body; and so we would say that God is grasped by nothing other than by what has been made in the image of that mind (Genesis 1:27). Now, to use Paul’s words, it is “through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And if I say “face,” let no one misrepresent, because of the word, the sense it conveys. Let him learn instead from the words “with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18), that in such places it is not a face of the senses that is meant, but one understood figuratively, like the eyes and ears and all the other things we showed above to share their names with the members of the body.

Man, then, that is, the soul using a body, which is called “the inner man” (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16) and also “soul,” answers not what Celsus wrote down but what the man of God himself teaches. A Christian would not use the voice of the flesh, since he has learned “by the Spirit to put to death the deeds of the body” (Romans 8:13), and “always to carry about in the body the dying of Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4:10), and “Put to death the members that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:5). He knows what is meant by “My Spirit shall not remain in these men for ever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3); he understands too that “those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8); and for this reason he does everything so as no longer to be at all “in the flesh, but” only “in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9).

choices.choice: ‘ἐπέκεινα νοῦ καὶ οὐσίας’ echoes Plato, Republic 509b (the Good ‘beyond being’), but it is Origen’s own phrase, not a quotation, so no inline citation. ‘τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἐκείνου τοῦ νοῦ εἰκόνα γενομένῳ’ alludes to Genesis 1:27 (LXX ‘κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ’); cited inline. 1 Corinthians 13:12 is quoted in compressed form (‘νῦν μὲν ... δι᾿ ἐσόπτρου καὶ ἐν αἰνίγματι τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον’); Origen’s ‘καὶ’ and Koetschau’s ’(ἐν)’ are both translated (‘through a mirror and in a riddle’). In 2 Corinthians 3:18 Origen’s text lacks Paul’s ‘ἡμεῖς δὲ πάντες’; the English supplies ‘we are’ only because the participle μεταμορφούμενοι needs a finite verb in English. ‘ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος’ occurs in Romans 7:22 and Ephesians 3:16 (cf. 2 Corinthians 4:16, ‘ὁ ἔσω ἡμῶν’). ‘ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος’ is ambiguous: either the Christian himself, as a man of God, or the scriptural ‘man of God’ (1 Timothy 6:11; 2 Timothy 3:17); kept literal and not cited inline. Colossians 3:5 is quoted without ‘ὑμῶν’, so no ‘your’ in the English. Genesis 6:3 is the Septuagint (‘οὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ ... ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τούτοις’), which differs from English Bibles made from the Hebrew (‘strive/abide’); rendered from the Greek (‘remain in these men’). Romans 8:9 is split by Origen (‘ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἀλλ᾿’ ... ‘ἐν’ μόνῳ ‘τῷ πνεύματι’); the quotation marks follow his split. ‘Spirit’ capitalised in Romans 8:13, Genesis 6:3 and Romans 8:9 as God’s Spirit.
1 Corinthians 13:12: dropped 'and' restored ('through a mirror and in a riddle')
added inline citation Genesis 1:27 for 'made in the image'
συκοφαντείτω clause: 'twist the meaning the word signifies because of the word itself' changed to 'misrepresent, because of the word, the sense it conveys'
Colossians 3:5: added 'your' removed (not in Origen's text)
Genesis 6:3 LXX: 'among these men' changed to 'in these men' (ἐν)
'So the man' changed to 'Man, then' (ἄνθρωπος μὲν οὖν, general)
